en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Bowls 21.
The Training Rule on Bowls:
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were accumulating many alms-bowls.
Seeing this, people wandering on a tour of the monastery complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can these ascetics, sons of the Sakyans, accumulate so many alms-bowls?"
“The ascetics, followers of the Sakyan son, will engage in the trade of cloth or set up a pottery shop,” so they complained, grumbled, and spread it about.
The monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... they complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
“How can the group-of-six monks keep an extra bowl?
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Blessed One asked:
“Is it true, monks, that you keep an extra bowl?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can you, foolish men, keep an extra bowl?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘Should any monk keep an extra almsbowl, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya).’”
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, an extra bowl had come into the possession of the Venerable Ānanda,
and the Venerable Ānanda desired to give that bowl to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta was staying at Sāketa.
Then, it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
"A training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One—"
‘An extra bowl is not to be kept.
Now this extra bowl has come into my possession,
and I wish to give this bowl to the Venerable Sāriputta.
"And the Venerable Sāriputta is staying at Sāketa.
How, indeed, should I proceed?
He reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“But how long will it be, Ānanda, before Sāriputta returns?
“In nine or ten days, Blessed One.
Then, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One gave a Dhamma talk and addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, monks, to keep an extra bowl for a maximum of ten days.
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘An extra bowl may be kept for a maximum of ten days. For one who keeps it beyond that, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.’”
"Up to ten days at most" means it should be kept for a maximum of ten days.
"An extra bowl" (atirekapatta) is as follows:
Not determined and not assigned.
"Bowl" means two kinds of bowls: an iron bowl and a clay bowl.
There are three grades of bowl: the superior bowl, the middling bowl, and the inferior bowl.
The superior bowl is said to hold half an *āḷhaka* of boiled rice, a fourth part of solid food, and a corresponding amount of curry.
The middling bowl is said to hold one *nāḷika* of boiled rice, a fourth part of solid food, and a corresponding amount of curry.
A "small" bowl is one that takes a portion of boiled rice equal to a quarter-measure, along with a corresponding amount of hard food and sauce.
Anything larger than that is "not small.
For one who exceeds that [limit], it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya).
At the rising of the sun on the eleventh day, it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment.
It must be relinquished to either the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
And this, monks, is how it should be relinquished.

That bhikkhu, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the elder bhikkhus, having sat down on his haunches and extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak thus:
"Venerable sirs, this bowl of mine has exceeded ten days and is to be relinquished.
I relinquish it to the Saṅgha."
Having relinquished it, the offense must be confessed.
A competent and capable monk should receive the confession of the offense,
and the relinquished bowl should be returned.
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This bowl, which was subject to relinquishment by the monk so-and-so, has been surrendered to the Saṅgha.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this bowl back to the monk so-and-so.”

That bhikkhu, having approached a number of bhikkhus, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed down at the feet of the elder bhikkhus, having sat down on his heels and raised his joined palms, should speak to them thus:
"Venerable sirs, this bowl of mine has exceeded ten days and is to be relinquished.
I relinquish it to the venerable ones."
Having relinquished it, the offense should be confessed.
A competent and capable monk should accept the confession of the offense,
and the relinquished bowl should be returned.
“Venerable sirs, let me address you.
This bowl, which was subject to relinquishment for the monk so-and-so, has been surrendered to you, venerable sirs.
If it seems appropriate to the venerable ones, may you give this bowl back to the monk so-and-so.”

That bhikkhu, having approached another bhikkhu, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down on his haunches, and having extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak to him thus:
"Friend, this bowl of mine has exceeded ten days and is to be relinquished.
I relinquish it to the Venerable One."
Having relinquished it, the offense must be confessed.
That monk must accept the offense,
and the relinquished bowl must be returned.
“I give this bowl to the Venerable One.
If ten days have passed and he perceives that they have passed, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If ten days have passed and he is in doubt, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If ten days have elapsed and he perceives that they have not elapsed, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya).
If the item has not been formally determined and he perceives that it has been determined, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If the item has not been assigned to another and he perceives that it has been assigned, it is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession.
If it has not been relinquished, but one perceives that it has been relinquished, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it has not been lost, but one perceives that it has been lost, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it has not been destroyed, but one perceives that it has been destroyed, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it is not split, but one perceives it as split, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If it is not stolen, but one perceives it as stolen, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one uses a bowl that has been forfeited without having forfeited it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If ten days have not elapsed, but he perceives that they have elapsed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If ten days have not elapsed, but he is uncertain, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If ten days have not elapsed, and he perceives that they have not elapsed, there is no offense.

There is no offense if, within ten days, one formally resolves upon it, assigns it to another, gives it away, it is lost, it is destroyed, it is broken, they take it after having stolen it, they take it on trust,
or in the case of one who is insane.
"Regarding the first offender":
Now at that time, the group of six monks did not give back a bowl that had been relinquished.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, an almsbowl that has been relinquished must not be given back. Whoever should give it back commits an offense of wrong-doing.
The first training rule on the almsbowl is finished.
